one_line.text: American scientist and writer whose work spans physiology, ecology, biogeography and continent-scale explanations of human societies.

biography.text: Born in Boston in 1937, Diamond studied at Harvard and completed a Cambridge doctorate. His scientific career began in physiology and expanded into evolutionary biology, ecology and biogeography, including extensive fieldwork in New Guinea. At UCLA he held roles across geography, physiology and public health. His general-reader books move from human evolution to environmental explanations of history, societal collapse, traditional societies and national crises.

background.text: Diamond approaches large historical questions through comparative natural experiments: islands, continents and populations become cases in which environmental differences may help explain divergent outcomes. New Guinea fieldwork supplied both local knowledge and the question that opens Guns, Germs, and Steel.

expertise.text: His direct research expertise includes integrative and evolutionary physiology, ecology and biogeography; UCLA also lists geography and human society among his research interests. He is an interdisciplinary synthesiser rather than a conventionally trained historian, so his claims about culture, institutions and particular regions need comparison with specialists in those fields.

perspective_and_limits.text: He deliberately shifts explanation away from racial difference and towards environmental starting conditions over very long timescales. This makes biogeographic constraints visible, but his natural-science method can compress human agency, cultural invention, institutions and conflict. William McNeill praised the new angle while arguing that Diamond treated cultural history as too automatic a product of environment.
